style: ONE single full-frame image, not a collage. 18th-century European copperplate engraving, hand-coloured with thin watercolour washes: black ink hatching and cross-hatching, sepia paper, muted ochre, rose, green and blue washes, like an illustration from a 1770 travel book about Siam. Wide 16:9 composition with the subject in the middle band. Dignified, no gore. No text, no letters, no numbers, no watermark, no frame border.
rules: Any Siamese king is seen from behind or far away, face not visible. Late-16th-century Siamese and Burmese costume unless the shot says otherwise.

shots.prompt: A Siamese king in gilded armour seen from behind pours water from a golden ewer onto the ground at a riverside camp, declaring independence; nobles and soldiers kneel around him, war elephants and banners behind.
Endless columns of Burmese soldiers and war elephants march across a plain toward the distant walls and prangs of Ayutthaya, smoke on the horizon, seen from a hill.
A Burmese crown prince on a richly decorated royal war elephant under a red tiered parasol leaves the gate of Pegu at the head of a great army, seen from behind, golden pagoda in the distance.
Three small white stupas stand on a forested mountain pass; a long column of soldiers and elephants winds down the jungle trail past them, misty ridges behind.
War elephants and soldiers ford a wide shallow river between jungle-covered limestone hills, bamboo rafts carrying supplies, the army stretching into the distance.
The Ayutthaya army marches out of a city gate with white walls and tall prangs: royal war elephants with white tiered parasols, spearmen, banners, heading west across dry rice fields.
Two royal war elephants in musth, dark fluid on their temples, trumpeting and pulling ahead; their mahouts strain with hooks, the riders hold on, dust rising on a dry plain.
Two royal elephants plunge alone into the middle of an enemy army in thick dust; only a handful of Siamese foot guards run behind them, enemy spears all around.
Through swirling dust, a Burmese crown prince sits on his royal war elephant under the shade of a large leafy tree, a red tiered parasol above him, his guards around him.
A Siamese king on a royal war elephant, seen from behind, raises his arm and calls out across the battlefield toward a Burmese prince on another elephant under a tree, both armies watching.
A second pair of war elephants clash tusk to tusk in the dust: a young Siamese prince on one, a Burmese general on the other, soldiers scattering around them.
The Burmese army breaks and retreats across a dusty plain, banners falling, elephants turning back, Siamese soldiers chasing.
Inside a Siamese palace hall with red pillars, army generals prostrate on the floor in shame before a king seated on a raised throne, seen from behind and far away.
A Siamese palace library burns at night: flames from carved wooden halls, palm-leaf manuscripts and folding paper books scattered and burning, smoke over the prangs of Ayutthaya.
A Siamese court scribe kneels at a low table writing a royal chronicle with a stylus in a long folding paper book, candlelight, stacks of manuscripts, 17th century.
A wide plain of central Siam seen from above with many small ponds full of green water weed and lotus, villages and palms between them, buffalo and farmers.
In a 1910s Siamese government study, an official in a white high-collared uniform seen from behind bends over old chronicles and a large hand-drawn map, oil lamp, bookshelves.
In 1913 a party of Siamese officials in white uniforms and pith helmets with local guides pushes through jungle and finds the overgrown brick base of a ruined stupa.
A 1914 royal procession of officials in white uniforms with parasols arrives on foot at a ruined brick stupa base in a forest clearing, villagers kneeling, seen from far away.
A huge new white bell-shaped stupa rises in bamboo scaffolding over the low ruin of an old brick stupa, workers carrying bricks, 1950s Thailand, rice fields around.
An ornate vintage engraved banknote design without any writing: an oval vignette of a king on a war elephant before a tall white stupa, guilloche patterns and borders.
A cutaway cross-section of a tall white bell-shaped stupa revealing a small old crumbling brick stupa base preserved inside it, architectural drawing style.
An ancient overgrown brick mound with old trees stands in green rice fields in western Thailand, low hills of Kanchanaburi behind, a farmer and buffalo nearby.
An ancient Dvaravati-era stupa ruin of large laterite blocks and bricks with stucco fragments, much older and weathered, in a quiet field at dusk.
1970s Thai scholars in shirts and glasses argue across a long wooden table covered with maps, photographs of ruins and stacks of newspapers, ceiling fan, a committee listening.
A bronze monument of a king riding a war elephant on a tall stone base in a park, limestone mountains of Kanchanaburi behind, people paying respect with flowers, seen from the side.
A very tall white stupa on a square stepped base rises alone among flooded rice fields north of Ayutthaya, palm trees, a boat on a canal.
A Burmese court chronicler writes on a long black folding parabaik book with a white steatite pencil, in a teak pavilion with a golden pagoda outside.
A Dutch East India Company merchant in black 17th-century clothes and white collar writes in a leather-bound journal at a desk in a trading house in Ayutthaya, ships on the river outside.
A smaller royal war elephant shies away from battle; a king on its back, seen from behind, sprinkles holy water from a small vessel over its head, monks' amulets, dust.
A great royal elephant adorned with gold cloth, a jewelled headdress and a white parasol is honoured in a palace courtyard; nobles kneel, offerings of flowers, a ceremony.
A Burmese general's elephant in musth breaks its blindfold and charges, while gun smoke from a musket drifts across two royal elephants in the background.
Portuguese mercenaries in morion helmets and breastplates fire matchlock muskets from among Asian troops, smoke clouds, war elephants in the distance.
Two royal war elephants locked head to head; one has been gored at the base of its tusk and sinks to its knees, dust and fallen parasols.
A Siamese court astrologer and a modern scholar compare a traditional lunar calendar chart of circles and segments drawn on a chalk board with a European calendar, no writing visible.
An empty dry plain at sunset where a battle happened long ago: no ruins, no walls, only wind-blown grass, a lone tree and distant hills.
